description: Design a persistent, named AI agent persona with a distinct voice, durable memory and clear operating rules, producing SOUL.md (personality), AGENTS.md (operating manual), MEMORY.md (cross-session knowledge) and BOOTSTRAP.md (first boot). Not for the engineering PRD and work orders of an agent system (use agent-prd) or a fellow's role / tools / memory / eval spec (use agent-design).

Interview the user and produce an Agent PRD plus engineering work orders: the planning documents that must exist before any agent code is written (job, checkable success criteria and first ten eval tasks, loop and stop condition, state and durability, context, memory, tools, guardrails, build order). Searchable UI/UX style database: recommend a complete design system for a product type (UI style, color palette, font pairing, UX guidelines, chart types) from 50+ styles, 161 palettes and 57 font pairings, and persist it as a master design-system file. Use when the user asks you to recommend or pick a style, palette and fonts for a new app, search a style database, or generate a design system for a product type such as a spa, fintech or e-commerce app. Not for token architecture or CSS variables (use ckm-design-system), adding color to an existing gray UI (use colorize), or agency-grade build directions (use impeccable).

Make a narrated video of what a merged pull request changed in a web app's UI — recordings of the real running app, before and after, with voiceover and captions — instead of reading code. Use when asked for a PR video, UI walkthrough, "what changed" video, release demo or before/after recording of a merged PR.

Find the real, durable need under a list of feature requests and rank the one to build for. Use when the user hands over a 'needs' list that is mostly features (integrations, dashboards, AI summaries, voice input) and asks what customers really need, to find the unmet or under-served need, which need to prioritise, or the real need under a feature request. Onions each stated need to a tech-invariant core, sorts survivors with Kano (must / performance / delighter) and returns one durable, under-served wedge need with its evidence, in a prioritised need map. NOT a general jobs, pains and gains map from interviews (use jobs-to-be-done), naming who holds the need or budget (use user-buyer-decider-map), reducing the job to its currencies (use job-in-primitives), or scoring the whole idea (use so-what-stress-test).

Run a moderated usability session on a working prototype and return findings tied to the screen, not the user. Fires on 'run a usability test', 'watch a user try it', 'usability protocol', 'can a first-time user complete X', 'see where they get stuck'. Product runs, Engineering watches muted, Design notes; tasks are framed as goals, the user is never led or asked 'do you like it', and every finding is scored on observed task success (behaviour 0.7), never stated preference (opinion 0.1). Output: a Usability Findings sheet with each defect tied to a step, counted across users, severity by frequency x blocking. NOT for building the prototype (use first-mocks), shadowing an expert to capture judgment (use tacit-knowledge-interview), or testing demand or willingness to pay (use wizard-of-oz-probe or concierge-probe).

Splits a buying situation into four distinct roles (which may share people) — user (feels the pain, touches the product), buyer (owns the budget line), decision-maker (final signature / veto), champion (spends internal capital to push it) — each pinned to ONE title, ONE budget (or an explicit none), ONE why-now. Fires on "who's the actual buyer", "who decides", "map the stakeholders", "map the buying committee", "the user loves it but who signs the cheque", "who's our champion and who can veto us". Output is a filled Stakeholder-Role Map that feeds the buyer-clarity row of problem-quality-scorecard. NOT the 8-dimension go/no-go (problem-quality-scorecard), NOT ranking which unmet need to build first (unserved-needs-finder), NOT a demographic day-in-the-life persona (proto-persona), NOT simulating users before interviews (synthetic-users).

Write development-ready user stories: a single story in Mike Cohn format (As a / I want to / so that) with Gherkin Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, or a full set of backlog stories for a feature using the 3 C's (Card, Conversation, Confirmation) and INVEST with numbered acceptance criteria and supplied design links. Use when writing a user story, breaking a feature into backlog items, converting a PRD requirement into stories, defining acceptance criteria, or writing situation-first job stories (When / I want to / so I can). Not for splitting an oversized story or epic (use user-story-splitting), or laying out the whole journey and release slices (use user-story-mapping).

Create a Jeff Patton user story map: backbone activities, steps and tasks laid out left-to-right as the user's journey, prioritized top-to-bottom, with release slices and a walking-skeleton MVP. Works as a one-shot map or as an interactive story-mapping workshop with adaptive questions and a facilitation agenda. Use when planning an MVP or release around a user workflow, turning a flat backlog into a map, aligning a team on scope, or running a story mapping session. Not for writing individual stories with acceptance criteria (use user-story), splitting one oversized story (use user-story-splitting), or quarter-level initiative sequencing (use roadmap-planning).
Break a large story or epic into smaller deliverable stories using proven split patterns. Use when backlog items are too big for estimation, sequencing, or independent release.

Go / no-go gate for launching a built v1 or pilot, on two recorded tests: a true stranger reaches first correct value in 60 seconds or less unaided, AND the learn-from-corrections mechanism is wired and proven to compound. Use when the user asks if they're ready to launch, whether v1 is good enough to ship, for a launch bar or go/no-go on a v1 or pilot, especially with time-to-value or corrections-loop evidence. Output: a recorded-evidence go / no-go checklist. Not the ongoing post-launch loop (use refine-flywheel), not pilot price or commercial terms (use pilot-six-term-sheet), not defining what 'working' means before code (use eval-first-spec).

Set the price and the charging metric for a validated product from MEASURED value: anchor the number at 10-20% of the measured incremental value per outcome, check it clears the cost per outcome, and charge on the outcome, asset or decision delivered, never on seats or tiers. Use when the user has pilot results or measured value (e.g. money recovered or hours saved per outcome) and asks to set the price, what to charge, what the number is, or per seat vs per outcome. Emits a value-priced model, or refuses and routes to measurement when value is unmeasured. Not for brainstorming revenue models or SaaS tiers and packaging (use pricing-strategy), structuring the whole pilot deal (use pilot-six-term-sheet), or measuring today's cost (use current-state-map).

Refactor React components with composition patterns: replace boolean-prop explosions with compound components, context providers and slots, design flexible component library APIs, and apply React 19 API changes. Use when the user says a component has too many boolean props or variants, asks to refactor a Modal, Card or Form API, or mentions compound components or render props. Not for performance (use vercel-react-best-practices).

Review and fix React and Next.js code for performance using Vercel's rules: request waterfalls and sequential awaits, server vs client components, data fetching, bundle size (heavy imports like lodash or moment), re-renders, memoization and caching. Use when the user asks to review or optimise a React or Next.js page or component for performance, mentions useEffect fetching, waterfalls or bundle bloat. Not for Vercel Web Interface Guidelines reviews (use audit) or component API design (use vercel-composition-patterns).

React Native and Expo performance and best practices: virtualised lists (FlashList), image handling, animations with Reanimated, native modules and platform APIs. Use when the user mentions React Native or Expo, a stuttering feed or list, dropped animation frames on Android or iOS, or mobile app performance. Not for web React (use vercel-react-best-practices).

Use when asked to make, redo or update a narrated demo, tutorial, onboarding or help video that tours a flow of a running web app, e.g. "record a video of signup through to the first project" or "make a help video for onboarding". Drives real Chrome with Playwright and outputs a 1080p MP4 with a smooth cursor, real typing and scrolling, eased zooms on form fields, title cards, an AI voiceover (Deepgram) and WebVTT captions. Not for videos of what a pull request changed or before/after comparisons; use ui-walkthrough for those.

Pressure-test ONE proposed wedge against five pass/fail thresholds (standalone value, forced cadence, travel, structural expansion, scoreable adoption) and return a 5-row verdict that calls it a real wedge only on 5/5. Fires on "is this a wedge", "is my wedge sharp enough", "what's my wedge", "the smallest thing that forces adoption", "will this actually get adopted". Not for defensibility over years (use moat-design-canvas), not for scoring the whole idea across eight dimensions (use problem-quality-scorecard), not for the one-glance so-what gut check (use so-what-stress-test).

Fires when a fellow wants a human to run the machine behind the curtain for a day to test usage — "fake the backend", "wizard of oz", "woz test", "human behind the curtain", "have a person answer the requests and see if they act on it". Output is a WoZ setup plus a result read-out that reports usage behaviour and an explicit "what this does NOT prove" section for feasibility, unit cost, and scale. NOT for choosing which probe to run (that is `probe-matrix`), NOT for testing whether a workflow reads on paper (that is `paper-sketch-probe`), and NOT for finding real cost-per-task (that is `agent-concierge-probe`).

Design a multi-agent workflow: which agents (researcher, analyst, drafter, critic, prototyper), the spawn trigger for each, how work hands off between them, and which surface each runs on (Claude.ai, Claude Code, Cowork). Use when the user or a fellow wants a fleet or team of agents, asks how several agents should work together or hand off, or wants to orchestrate agents for recurring work like weekly research. Not for one agent's role, tools and memory (use agent-design).

Find the proprietary data a product can own that a competitor or foundation model can't get. Use when the user lists candidate data sources (manuals, logs, work orders, WhatsApp threads, sensor feeds, public videos) or asks what data they actually own, where their proprietary data is, what data a competitor can't get, or how to build the moat's data seed. Sorts every source by one test, can a foundation model already reach it, and keeps only workflow-trapped, permission-gated signal (shadow AI threads, operational logs, permits, vendor-locked sensor feeds, workflow exhaust) as the moat seed, in a sourced corpus map. Not for drafting the contract that unlocks a gated source (use data-rights-clause), scoring one signal as evidence (use evidence-ladder), or capturing tacit judgment (use tacit-knowledge-interview).
